event_description: Severe Weather occurring on April 18, 2025 (Buena Vista, Fremont, Page, and Plymouth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm air advection increased across the area through the day with a warm front draped across northern Iowa by the afternoon. Meanwhile a cold front was approaching Iowa from the northwest. Storms developed in the early evening in far southwest Iowa, moving across southern Iowa through late evening and overnight. Initial storms were surface based with CAPE exceeding 2000 J/kg and sweeping low level curvature in hodographs. Rotating updrafts supported hail growth with initial surface based storms resulting in a tornado in Union County. Storms became elevated overnight but remained strong, fueled by a strong 70+ knot low level jet.  As storms in southern Iowa tapered off overnight additional storms developed along the boundary there. These storms became quite strong, producing golf ball to baseball sized hail from around 2 AM and lasting until after 5 AM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Largest hail up to one inch in diameter.

Storms in far southeast South Dakota and northeast Nebraska produced spotty large hail, with a more intense cluster of both hail (up to 2.5 inches diameter) and wind (to around 80 mph) producing storms moving through northwest Iowa during the couple hours after midnight.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on April 18, 2025 (Buena Vista, Fremont, Page, and Plymouth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On April 17, 2025, two powerful and long-lived supercells swept across eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa during the afternoon and evening hours, bringing significant severe weather impacts. The event was driven by a dynamic upper-level pattern, including a compact shortwave trough that helped spin up a surface low near the Nebraska-Kansas border. This low tracked eastward through the day, accompanied by a surface cold front advancing from the northwest and a dryline bulging into southeast Nebraska.||Ahead of these features, strong southerly flow transported warm, moist air into the region. Temperatures rose into the 80s, with dewpoints climbing into the mid-50s to low 60s. These conditions yielded moderate instability, with MUCAPE values ranging from 1000 to 2000 J/kg. Vertical wind shear was notably favorable for organized convection, with deep-layer shear in the 50���60 kt range and strong low-level hodograph curvature supporting supercell development.||Two discrete supercells initiated in eastern Nebraska during the late afternoon and tracked eastward into western Iowa during the evening. The northern supercell initially developed near Columbus, Nebraska, and tracked east through Colfax, Dodge, Washington, and Douglas counties before entering Pottawattamie County, Iowa. It produced large hail, with reports of stones up to 4 inches in diameter, and caused widespread wind-driven hail damage. The storm also spawned an EF-3 tornado that impacted portions of Douglas and Washington counties.||The second and southern-most storm formed north of Seward, Nebraska, and moved eastward across Seward, Lancaster, and Cass counties before crossing into Fremont and Page counties in Iowa later in the evening. Along its path, the storm produced baseball-sized hail (up to 2.75 inches) and several tornadoes. In Cass County, Nebraska, three tornadoes were reported���two rated EF-0 and one rated EF-U. After crossing into Iowa, the storm produced an EF-0 tornado in Fremont County, followed shortly by a stronger EF-1 tornado in Page County. This tornado grew to a maximum width of 1,971 yards before dissipating. Additionally, damaging winds associated with the storm���s rear-flank downdraft reached up to 86 mph in Page County. Both storms continued into southwest Iowa during the evening before gradually weakening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media report of hail measured up to 2.25 in diameter.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on April 18, 2025 (Buena Vista, Fremont, Page, and Plymouth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms lifted north northeastward along the Mississippi River through the Quad Cites with an area of trailing stratiform rainfall behind it. There were scattered reports of thunderstorm wind damage in the counties along the Mississippi River. A microburst occurred near West Burlington that caused damage to  a DOT Shet and broke several power poles. An NWS Storm Survey team found damage in this area consistent with wind speeds of 80 to 90 mph. In addition to the severe thunderstorms, heavy rainfall of 2 to 3 inches fell across western Johnson and southwest Linn Counties. This led to reports of flash flooding in western Cedar Rapids, Hiawatha, and Marion.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 911 Dispatcher relayed a report of a tree that fell on a parked vehicle. The time of the event was estimated using radar.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on April 18, 2025 (Buena Vista, Fremont, Page, and Plymouth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm air advection increased across the area through the day with a warm front draped across northern Iowa by the afternoon. Meanwhile a cold front was approaching Iowa from the northwest. Storms developed in the early evening in far southwest Iowa, moving across southern Iowa through late evening and overnight. Initial storms were surface based with CAPE exceeding 2000 J/kg and sweeping low level curvature in hodographs. Rotating updrafts supported hail growth with initial surface based storms resulting in a tornado in Union County. Storms became elevated overnight but remained strong, fueled by a strong 70+ knot low level jet.  As storms in southern Iowa tapered off overnight additional storms developed along the boundary there. These storms became quite strong, producing golf ball to baseball sized hail from around 2 AM and lasting until after 5 AM.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on June 11, 2025 (Osceola and Palo Alto Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface boundary oriented roughly west southwest to east northeast over northern Iowa provided a genesis region for thunderstorms on June 11 2025. Storms developing along this boundary moved into a very unstable environment south and east of the boundary, boasting MLCAPE values of 2500 to 3000 J/kg. Most of the better wind shear was located along and north of this boundary, but effective shear values of 30 to 40 kts along and just south of this boundary were sufficient for organized storms. Surface temperatures were also quite warm in the warm sector, with afternoon temperatures in the 90s but dewpoints only in the upper 50s to low 60s, resulting in inverted-V soundings and an environment conducive for strong cool production and downburst winds. Thunderstorms were initially discrete, producing strong downburst winds and hail. One storm in far northern Iowa, nearest to the boundary and within a more sheared environment, exhibited supercellular characteristics and produced a very strong rear-flank downdraft (RFD). Wind gusts of over 70 mph were observed with this RFD, some of which extended multiple miles south of the main storm. Personal weather stations showed a nearly 30 degree Fahrenheit temperature drop and 5 to 10 millibar pressure increase accompanying these winds as the RFD/cold pool passed through. The strong winds resulted in tree and building damage beginning near Emmetsburg through Algona and into Belmond. Another storm near Dows produced a healthy core which promptly collapsed, producing a microburst which damaged a machine shed on a farm outside Dows. Upon reaching north central Iowa, storms began to grow upscale as cold pools congealed, transitioning into a linear mode. While this transition occurred, the gust front began to outrun the storms, but continued to produce strong 50 to 60 mph winds as it trudged eastward. A plume of dust accompanied this gust front upon it's arrival in northeastern Iowa. Eventually, storms reoriented themselves along the leading edge of the cold pool, producing more tree damage and power outages throughout the Cedar Falls/Waterloo area. Strong winds continued into Tama county and eastern Black Hawk county, where a semi truck and trailer was overturned on Highway 20. Storms eventually departed the DMX forecast area in the early evening, but continued producing strong winds as they moved through eastern Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust measured by personal weather station.

With mixed-layer instability of 1500-2000 J/kg and deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots, organized storms developed and utilized an inverted-V thermodynamic profile to accentuate a swath of damaging wind gusts near and just south of Iowa State Highway 9.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two trees were blown down along 280th Street west of Fostoria.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on June 11, 2025 (Osceola and Palo Alto Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed along a stout outflow boundary, which dropped southward into the area through the day. The boundary served as a gradient in shear and instability, and focused initial development during the afternoon hours, which featured hail up to golf ball size. Storms evolved to produce a couple tracks of damaging wind heading southeast across northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa into very early evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Winds were measured by a personal weather station.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on June 11, 2025 (Osceola and Palo Alto Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface boundary oriented roughly west southwest to east northeast over northern Iowa provided a genesis region for thunderstorms on June 11 2025. Storms developing along this boundary moved into a very unstable environment south and east of the boundary, boasting MLCAPE values of 2500 to 3000 J/kg. Most of the better wind shear was located along and north of this boundary, but effective shear values of 30 to 40 kts along and just south of this boundary were sufficient for organized storms. Surface temperatures were also quite warm in the warm sector, with afternoon temperatures in the 90s but dewpoints only in the upper 50s to low 60s, resulting in inverted-V soundings and an environment conducive for strong cool production and downburst winds. Thunderstorms were initially discrete, producing strong downburst winds and hail. One storm in far northern Iowa, nearest to the boundary and within a more sheared environment, exhibited supercellular characteristics and produced a very strong rear-flank downdraft (RFD). Wind gusts of over 70 mph were observed with this RFD, some of which extended multiple miles south of the main storm. Personal weather stations showed a nearly 30 degree Fahrenheit temperature drop and 5 to 10 millibar pressure increase accompanying these winds as the RFD/cold pool passed through. The strong winds resulted in tree and building damage beginning near Emmetsburg through Algona and into Belmond. Another storm near Dows produced a healthy core which promptly collapsed, producing a microburst which damaged a machine shed on a farm outside Dows. Upon reaching north central Iowa, storms began to grow upscale as cold pools congealed, transitioning into a linear mode. While this transition occurred, the gust front began to outrun the storms, but continued to produce strong 50 to 60 mph winds as it trudged eastward. A plume of dust accompanied this gust front upon it's arrival in northeastern Iowa. Eventually, storms reoriented themselves along the leading edge of the cold pool, producing more tree damage and power outages throughout the Cedar Falls/Waterloo area. Strong winds continued into Tama county and eastern Black Hawk county, where a semi truck and trailer was overturned on Highway 20. Storms eventually departed the DMX forecast area in the early evening, but continued producing strong winds as they moved through eastern Iowa.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on June 11, 2025 (Osceola and Palo Alto Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface boundary oriented roughly west southwest to east northeast over northern Iowa provided a genesis region for thunderstorms on June 11 2025. Storms developing along this boundary moved into a very unstable environment south and east of the boundary, boasting MLCAPE values of 2500 to 3000 J/kg. Most of the better wind shear was located along and north of this boundary, but effective shear values of 30 to 40 kts along and just south of this boundary were sufficient for organized storms. Surface temperatures were also quite warm in the warm sector, with afternoon temperatures in the 90s but dewpoints only in the upper 50s to low 60s, resulting in inverted-V soundings and an environment conducive for strong cool production and downburst winds. Thunderstorms were initially discrete, producing strong downburst winds and hail. One storm in far northern Iowa, nearest to the boundary and within a more sheared environment, exhibited supercellular characteristics and produced a very strong rear-flank downdraft (RFD). Wind gusts of over 70 mph were observed with this RFD, some of which extended multiple miles south of the main storm. Personal weather stations showed a nearly 30 degree Fahrenheit temperature drop and 5 to 10 millibar pressure increase accompanying these winds as the RFD/cold pool passed through. The strong winds resulted in tree and building damage beginning near Emmetsburg through Algona and into Belmond. Another storm near Dows produced a healthy core which promptly collapsed, producing a microburst which damaged a machine shed on a farm outside Dows. Upon reaching north central Iowa, storms began to grow upscale as cold pools congealed, transitioning into a linear mode. While this transition occurred, the gust front began to outrun the storms, but continued to produce strong 50 to 60 mph winds as it trudged eastward. A plume of dust accompanied this gust front upon it's arrival in northeastern Iowa. Eventually, storms reoriented themselves along the leading edge of the cold pool, producing more tree damage and power outages throughout the Cedar Falls/Waterloo area. Strong winds continued into Tama county and eastern Black Hawk county, where a semi truck and trailer was overturned on Highway 20. Storms eventually departed the DMX forecast area in the early evening, but continued producing strong winds as they moved through eastern Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust measured by a personal weather station.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 10, 2025 (Scott County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The atmosphere on July 11, 2025, was primed for heavy rainfall, featuring a slow-moving frontal boundary that tapped into a corridor of abundant moisture to its south. This boundary, combined with strong instability, shear oriented along the boundary, and lift from an approaching upper-level disturbance, created an environment highly favorable for slow-moving, training thunderstorms capable of producing extremely high rainfall rates.||Torrential rainfall impacted much of the forecast area, but impacts were most notable in Black Hawk County where 2 to 3 inches of rain fell over a few hours. By early afternoon, the excessive rainfall rates overwhelmed drainage systems, and reports of flash flooding began to emerge from Waterloo and surrounding areas. Local emergency management, media, and storm spotters reported closed roadways due to high water. Some vehicles became stranded in the flooded roads, which had curb-deep water in many areas. Water was slow to recede for several hours after the heaviest rain had ended, leading to impacts continuing into the early evening.||In addition to the heavy rainfall, the atmosphere was also conducive for severe weather, but impacts were primarily in eastern and northeastern Iowa. One storm passing near the Iowa Speedway in Newton, IA prompted an evacuation from the speedway as IndyCar races were ongoing that weekend. The supercell produced a highly visible, rotating wall cloud and other ominous-looking features, but never produced a confirmed tornado or any significant damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Black Hawk EM, broadcast media, and local spotters reported roadways closed due to flooding, stranded vehicles, and water up to the curb on roadways in and around Waterloo. Public reports in Waterloo and Cedar Falls of swift moving water in low lying areas, as well as water bubbling out of manhole covers.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 (Hancock, O'Brien, Osceola, Sioux Counties)

Consequently, this portion of the line quickly became outflow-dominant, which limited the threat of widespread wind damage. However, the environment remained conducive for strong downburst winds, which occurred sporadically as new updrafts developed along the line through north-central into central Iowa. event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 (Hancock, O'Brien, Osceola, Sioux Counties)

The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several tree branches down blocking roads in town. Time estimated by radar.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 (Hancock, O'Brien, Osceola, Sioux Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A late-night Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) tracked southeastward through central Iowa from the night of July 27th into the morning of July 28th. This line of storms moved through a highly unstable environment, characterized by CAPE values of 4000 to 5000 J/kg. Effective wind shear was also favorable for organized severe weather, with 35 to 45 kts of shear ahead of the line. The structure of the system allowed areas along the eastern fringe, tracking east-southeastward, to remain balanced with the environment and produce strong winds across northern Iowa. Widespread crop, tree, and powerline damage was reported from straight-line winds throughout Winnebago, Hancock, Cerro Gordo, and Worth counties. Thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were measured, with a 71 mph wind gust at the Mason City Municipal Airport.|The portion of the line tracking more southward was oriented from east to west. This orientation was less favorable for system organization, as the wind shear vectors were parallel to the cold pool. Consequently, this portion of the line quickly became outflow-dominant, which limited the threat of widespread wind damage. However, the environment remained conducive for strong downburst winds, which occurred sporadically as new updrafts developed along the line through north-central into central Iowa. Many of these downbursts were near or slightly below severe limits, generally producing small tree branch damage, including within the Des Moines metro area. However, pockets of severe winds causing tree damage still occurred within this less organized portion of the storm.|Behind the initial line, a few clusters of storms oriented from north to south tracked east-southeastward, taking advantage of a more favorable shear orientation. One of these storms produced a 66 mph wind gust in Emmet County. However, these trailing storms generally remained sub-severe as they developed in the more stable, rain-cooled air behind the initial MCS.|After reaching Interstate 80 around 2:00 AM on July 28th, the storms became disorganized, and only general, non-severe thunderstorms continued southward through the remainder of the morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust measured by the Mason City ASOS.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 (Hancock, O'Brien, Osceola, Sioux Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station gust to 58 mph.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 (Hancock, O'Brien, Osceola, Sioux Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge was in place across the area, creating a hot and humid environment that was deeply unstable with MLCAPE of 3000-4500 J/kg even through the overnight hours when storms passed across Iowa. Sub-severe storms developed on the evening of July 29th associated with a stationary boundary that was draped across the state, but with little available shear they were disorganized. Meanwhile, a shortwave riding along the ridge pushed in from the west and reached western Iowa after midnight. This upper level support helped to organize the earlier convection into a line of storms in eastern Iowa while the primary line of storms organized in western Iowa. Both resulted in winds gusting 55-65+ mph as they swept across the state, leaving behind broken and uprooted trees that damaged homes in a couple cases.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 68 mph gust at a Personal Weather Station.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 (Hancock, O'Brien, Osceola, Sioux Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines down around Fort Dodge. Delayed report relayed by broadcast media. Time estimated by radar.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 (Hancock, O'Brien, Osceola, Sioux Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A late-night Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) tracked southeastward through central Iowa from the night of July 27th into the morning of July 28th. This line of storms moved through a highly unstable environment, characterized by CAPE values of 4000 to 5000 J/kg. Effective wind shear was also favorable for organized severe weather, with 35 to 45 kts of shear ahead of the line. The structure of the system allowed areas along the eastern fringe, tracking east-southeastward, to remain balanced with the environment and produce strong winds across northern Iowa. Widespread crop, tree, and powerline damage was reported from straight-line winds throughout Winnebago, Hancock, Cerro Gordo, and Worth counties. Thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were measured, with a 71 mph wind gust at the Mason City Municipal Airport.|The portion of the line tracking more southward was oriented from east to west. This orientation was less favorable for system organization, as the wind shear vectors were parallel to the cold pool. Consequently, this portion of the line quickly became outflow-dominant, which limited the threat of widespread wind damage. However, the environment remained conducive for strong downburst winds, which occurred sporadically as new updrafts developed along the line through north-central into central Iowa. Many of these downbursts were near or slightly below severe limits, generally producing small tree branch damage, including within the Des Moines metro area. However, pockets of severe winds causing tree damage still occurred within this less organized portion of the storm.|Behind the initial line, a few clusters of storms oriented from north to south tracked east-southeastward, taking advantage of a more favorable shear orientation. One of these storms produced a 66 mph wind gust in Emmet County. However, these trailing storms generally remained sub-severe as they developed in the more stable, rain-cooled air behind the initial MCS.|After reaching Interstate 80 around 2:00 AM on July 28th, the storms became disorganized, and only general, non-severe thunderstorms continued southward through the remainder of the morning.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)

This line of storms moved through a highly unstable environment, characterized by CAPE values of 4000 to 5000 J/kg. Effective wind shear was also favorable for organized severe weather, with 35 to 45 kts of shear ahead of the line. The structure of the system allowed areas along the eastern fringe, tracking east-southeastward, to remain balanced with the environment and produce strong winds across northern Iowa. Widespread crop, tree, and powerline damage was reported from straight-line winds throughout Winnebago, Hancock, Cerro Gordo, and Worth counties. Thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were measured, with a 71 mph wind gust at the Mason City Municipal Airport.|The portion of the line tracking more southward was oriented from east to west. This orientation was less favorable for system organization, as the wind shear vectors were parallel to the cold pool. Consequently, this portion of the line quickly became outflow-dominant, which limited the threat of widespread wind damage. However, the environment remained conducive for strong downburst winds, which occurred sporadically as new updrafts developed along the line through north-central into central Iowa. Many of these downbursts were near or slightly below severe limits, generally producing small tree branch damage, including within the Des Moines metro area. However, pockets of severe winds causing tree damage still occurred within this less organized portion of the storm.|Behind the initial line, a few clusters of storms oriented from north to south tracked east-southeastward, taking advantage of a more favorable shear orientation. One of these storms produced a 66 mph wind gust in Emmet County. However, these trailing storms generally remained sub-severe as they developed in the more stable, rain-cooled air behind the initial MCS.|After reaching Interstate 80 around 2:00 AM on July 28th, the storms became disorganized, and only general, non-severe thunderstorms continued southward through the remainder of the morning.

event_description: Severe Weather and Flooding occurring on July 17, 2025 (Hancock County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct supercell clusters developed across central South Dakota during the late afternoon of July 28 within a highly unstable environment (MUCAPE up to 5000 J/kg) ahead of an eastward advancing surface front. The southern supercell cluster produced three tornadoes across Gregory County, the strongest of which was rated EF2. ||Scattered severe wind gusts were reported across southeast South Dakota as the thunderstorms moved east before the two clusters merged near and south of Sioux Falls. Aided by increasing deep layer shear from the north, a linear structure rapidly developed with a derecho racing eastward into northwest Iowa. Winds gusted from 80 to 100 mph along the derecho's path with widespread tree and structural damage across the area. In addition, three embedded short-lived tornadoes were documented within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 60 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at Storm Lake Municipal Airport (KSLB).

event_description: Severe Weather and Flooding occurring on July 17, 2025 (Hancock County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal Weather Station gust to 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge was in place across the area, creating a hot and humid environment that was deeply unstable with MLCAPE of 3000-4500 J/kg even through the overnight hours when storms passed across Iowa. Sub-severe storms developed on the evening of July 29th associated with a stationary boundary that was draped across the state, but with little available shear they were disorganized. Meanwhile, a shortwave riding along the ridge pushed in from the west and reached western Iowa after midnight. This upper level support helped to organize the earlier convection into a line of storms in eastern Iowa while the primary line of storms organized in western Iowa. Both resulted in winds gusting 55-65+ mph as they swept across the state, leaving behind broken and uprooted trees that damaged homes in a couple cases.

These thunderstorms quickly grew upscale into a line, producing 55 to 75 mph wind gusts across southeast South Dakota and extreme northeast Nebraska, resulting in isolated tree damage. In addition, prolonged heavy rain resulted in some localized flash flooding across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by a personal weather station.

event_description: Severe Weather and Flooding occurring on July 17, 2025 (Hancock County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station gust to 63 mph.

event_description: Severe Weather and Flooding occurring on July 17, 2025 (Hancock County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A late-night Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) tracked southeastward through central Iowa from the night of July 27th into the morning of July 28th. This line of storms moved through a highly unstable environment, characterized by CAPE values of 4000 to 5000 J/kg. Effective wind shear was also favorable for organized severe weather, with 35 to 45 kts of shear ahead of the line. The structure of the system allowed areas along the eastern fringe, tracking east-southeastward, to remain balanced with the environment and produce strong winds across northern Iowa. Widespread crop, tree, and powerline damage was reported from straight-line winds throughout Winnebago, Hancock, Cerro Gordo, and Worth counties. Thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were measured, with a 71 mph wind gust at the Mason City Municipal Airport.|The portion of the line tracking more southward was oriented from east to west. This orientation was less favorable for system organization, as the wind shear vectors were parallel to the cold pool. Consequently, this portion of the line quickly became outflow-dominant, which limited the threat of widespread wind damage. However, the environment remained conducive for strong downburst winds, which occurred sporadically as new updrafts developed along the line through north-central into central Iowa. Many of these downbursts were near or slightly below severe limits, generally producing small tree branch damage, including within the Des Moines metro area. However, pockets of severe winds causing tree damage still occurred within this less organized portion of the storm.|Behind the initial line, a few clusters of storms oriented from north to south tracked east-southeastward, taking advantage of a more favorable shear orientation. One of these storms produced a 66 mph wind gust in Emmet County. However, these trailing storms generally remained sub-severe as they developed in the more stable, rain-cooled air behind the initial MCS.|After reaching Interstate 80 around 2:00 AM on July 28th, the storms became disorganized, and only general, non-severe thunderstorms continued southward through the remainder of the morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree branches down in Urbandale due to collapsing storm.

event_description: Severe Weather and Flooding occurring on July 17, 2025 (Hancock County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of July 29, 2026, a surface front draped from central Nebraska to the state's northeast and southeastern South Dakota, serving as the focal point for thunderstorm development during the late afternoon. As the evening progressed, these storms coalesced into a mesoscale convective complex (MCS) that moved southeast across eastern Nebraska and southwestern Iowa. While the atmosphere was primed with sufficient instability, a lack of shear remained a limiting factor for widespread storm organization. Regardless, several reports of damaging wind gusts ranging from 58 to 70 mph were received throughout the evening. A notable report came from a trained spotter 3 miles west of Westphalia, Iowa, who measured a 70 mph gust. Damage was also reported, including 6- to 8-inch diameter tree limbs downed in Murray, Nebraska.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter measured wind gust using a handheld anemometer. Had consistent 45-55 mph gusts and one gust of 70 mph.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Plymouth County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge was in place across the area, creating a hot and humid environment that was deeply unstable with MLCAPE of 3000-4500 J/kg even through the overnight hours when storms passed across Iowa. Sub-severe storms developed on the evening of July 29th associated with a stationary boundary that was draped across the state, but with little available shear they were disorganized. Meanwhile, a shortwave riding along the ridge pushed in from the west and reached western Iowa after midnight. This upper level support helped to organize the earlier convection into a line of storms in eastern Iowa while the primary line of storms organized in western Iowa. Both resulted in winds gusting 55-65+ mph as they swept across the state, leaving behind broken and uprooted trees that damaged homes in a couple cases.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 60 mph gust at a personal weather station.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Plymouth County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station gust to 58 mph.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Plymouth County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge was in place across the area, creating a hot and humid environment that was deeply unstable with MLCAPE of 3000-4500 J/kg even through the overnight hours when storms passed across Iowa. Sub-severe storms developed on the evening of July 29th associated with a stationary boundary that was draped across the state, but with little available shear they were disorganized. Meanwhile, a shortwave riding along the ridge pushed in from the west and reached western Iowa after midnight. This upper level support helped to organize the earlier convection into a line of storms in eastern Iowa while the primary line of storms organized in western Iowa. Both resulted in winds gusting 55-65+ mph as they swept across the state, leaving behind broken and uprooted trees that damaged homes in a couple cases.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Plymouth County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines down around Fort Dodge. Delayed report relayed by broadcast media. Time estimated by radar.

event_description: Severe Weather and Flooding occurring on August 17, 2025 (Chickasaw, Winnebago, Winneshiek Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak shortwave moved across Iowa overnight and through the morning of August 18th. The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms brought large to giant hail to portions of northeast Iowa during the afternoon on April 14th. The most notable storm in northeast Iowa was a left-moving supercell which brought hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter to portions of Charles City and into Howard County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local fire and rescue in Alta Vista reported golf ball sized hail.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on April 13 and continuing(Buchanan, Clay, Henry, Palo Alto and Plymouth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Various hail sizes up to a maximum of quarter size fell for a few minutes.

One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed a little less than one mile north of Webb just east of 290th Avenue in an open field.  The tornado was documented by numerous individuals as it tracked east-northeast for a little over a minute. The tornado crossed 300th Avenue near a farmstead where trees were damaged along the north side of the property and the resultant winds caused minor damage to the residence.  The tornado continued toward the east-northeast for a little over a minute over open fields and lifted just before 310th Avenue south of 470th Street. The tornado was rated EF0 with a maximum estimated wind speed of 75 mph. The average path width was 30 yards.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on April 13 and continuing(Buchanan, Clay, Henry, Palo Alto and Plymouth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.

Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on April 13 and continuing(Carroll, Crawford, Grundy, Harrison, and Washington Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. ||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph, and a tornado was confirmed near Little Sioux as a supercell approached the frontal boundary and underwent a storm merger. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter and spawned three brief tornadoes in southwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video and photo evidence of a small tornado near this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. ||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph, and a tornado was confirmed near Little Sioux as a supercell approached the frontal boundary and underwent a storm merger. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter and spawned three brief tornadoes in southwest Iowa.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on April 13 and continuing(Carroll, Crawford, Grundy, Harrison, and Washington Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong thunderstorms moved across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois and produced 50+ mph winds, causing some areas of damage to trees, roofs, and a few outbuildings. These were most pronounced to the immediate south of mesovortices (small scale circulations within the thunderstorm line that can in themselves result in tornadoes). Based on the nature of damage, observations, and radar, these reflect 65-80 mph wind gusts.||Two main areas of damage that experienced enhanced wind surges were:  1.) Kalona, IA (Washington Co)  and 2.) the east-southeast side of Iowa City (Johnson County).||A third area of isolated wind damage from Miles to Sabula, IA (Jackson County) was a little different in that it was much more of an outflow surging from decaying storms, but again straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Out building roof and walls damaged along with a grain bin. The time was estimated using radar data.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on April 13 and continuing(Carroll, Crawford, Grundy, Harrison, and Washington Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. ||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph, and a tornado was confirmed near Little Sioux as a supercell approached the frontal boundary and underwent a storm merger. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter and spawned three brief tornadoes in southwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two spotter reports confirmed a funnel with rotating dust at ground level with minor tree damage at one location. The track was mainly over open fields. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 70 mph.

Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska, eventually pushing into southwest Iowa by 4:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster.||The primary hazards with this portion of the severe complex were large hail and significant straight-line winds. Residents in communities such as Farragut and College Springs reported hail up to ping-pong ball size (1.50 inches). Meanwhile, the bowing segments of the storm complex continued to produce extreme downdrafts, highlighted by an 84 mph wind gust measured by a personal weather station northeast of Shambaugh. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts across southwest Iowa on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. As the severe squall line pushed across the Missouri River into western Iowa during the mid-to-late evening hours of May 17, it maintained its intensity and continued to produce damaging straight-line winds. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska, eventually pushing into southwest Iowa by 4:00 PM CST. Residents in communities such as Farragut and College Springs reported hail up to ping-pong ball size (1.50 inches). Meanwhile, the bowing segments of the storm complex continued to produce extreme downdrafts, highlighted by an 84 mph wind gust measured by a personal weather station northeast of Shambaugh. The storms tracked eastward into the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail estimated up to 1.50 inches in diameter.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on May 15 and continuing(Emmet, Hancock, Palo Alto, Plymouth, Pocahontas, Winnebago, Woodbury, and Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a strong wave sheared northward through the Dakotas, the right entrance region of an upper level jet interacted with a slow moving surface boundary to increase late day backing of wind fields and convergence.  While overall thermodynamic parameters were lacking, favorable overlap of near-surface vorticity and acceleration of near-surface parcels resulted in low-level rotating storms.  One storm anchored near the boundary produced a brief tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A very brief tornado touchdown was documented by two independent photos. The tornado  spun up briefly in open areas between the Little Sioux River and Morgan Trail to the north of Oto.  After traveling north for less than a minute, the tornado lifted just prior to crossing Morgan Trail.  The average path width was estimated at 30 yards.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on May 15 and continuing(Cherokee, Clay, Kossuth, Montgomery, and Ringgold Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak wave in northwest flow aloft enhanced the low-level jet into southeast South Dakota with moisture and better deep-layer shear arriving by late day near a weak frontal boundary. With mixed-layer instability from 1500-2200 J/kg and marginally supportive deep layer shear of 40-45 kts, isolated supercells developed with mainly hail from stronger cells up to 2 inches in diameter.
